body: One possible solution is to add build tags to avoid building with `hashicorp/raft` and `rclone`.
the binary size reduced from 95,571,392 bytes to 65,955,760 bytes with https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/commit/7a50762b9ed05f1410a24f52571b49a25cd561eb

@chrislusf Hello, the big binary does not affect the latency of request processing?
What risks are there if I use a large binary with the full tag?

> Avoid building with `hashicorp/raft` and `rclone`.

Does that mean that the rclone feature simply _disappears_ for the end user (e.g. me)?
Only to save a few tens of megabytes (when uncompressed) on disk?
If that's the case, as a the contributor and user of this rclone feature, I strongly object to this choice.
Tons of other Go applications are well within the reach of 80-100 MB (uncompressed) on disk, and I don't think that bothers a lot of people, does it?

Edit: it looks like I jumped too soon to the wrong conclusion, as `rclone` would still be part of the `full` distribution.
Well, actually, only partially, because:
1. it looks like this `full` distribution is only available for `linux/amd64`; why is that so?
2. the Docker image that you maintain at https://hub.docker.com/r/chrislusf/seaweedfs/ relies on `chrislusf/seaweedfs/releases/download/.*/linux_$ARCH.tar.gz"` so `rclone` would also disappear from this image as well, and I would have to maintain my own.

> * it looks like this `full` distribution is only available for `linux/amd64`; why is that so?
> * the Docker image that you maintain at https://hub.docker.com/r/chrislusf/seaweedfs/ relies on `chrislusf/seaweedfs/releases/download/.*/linux_$ARCH.tar.gz"` so `rclone` would also disappear from this image as well, and I would have to maintain my own.

which build you need?

I'm not sure what you mean by *build*, or if what _I_ (as a specific individual) need is the determining factor here.
It's more like that, as a _generic_ user of SeaweedFS (or any other software for that matter), I'd like to have consistency in the feature set that I can expect from SeaweedFS, independently of its build or distribution channel.
So should I download the, say, Linux/Mac, or x86/ARM version, I should be able to rely on the fact that SeaweedFS offers the same features. Including when it comes to "official" Docker images.
And it goes further than that, for example with Linux distributions. If package maintainers are faced with a choice of 4 flavours of SeaweedFS (combinations of large vs not large; full vs not full), what I can expect to get when I install it in my Linux distribution?
I don't know the technical details of why there already was this distinction between large vs not large builds.
But adding yet another dimension to this "build matrix" seems to lead to even more fragmentation in my opinion.

>   14 MB github.com/Azure/azure-storage-blob-go/azblob

[azure-storage-blob-go](https://github.com/Azure/azure-storage-blob-go?tab=readme-ov-file) is dead and should be replaced with [`github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/storage/azblob`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-go/tree/main/sdk/storage/azblob#readme) which is already included indirectly, I think from KMS? So that would save a chunk.
